title: Nicholas Winton's Scrapbook
text:
In December 1938 Nicholas Winton, a 29 year old London stockbroker, cancelled a skiing holiday to visit a friend in Prague who was helping refugees. Germany had just taken the Sudetenland, and families who had fled the Nazis were crowded into camps around the city. Winton saw that Jewish children were in particular danger and that no one was organizing to get them out of Czechoslovakia.

Back in London, working from his home after office hours with his mother and a small team, he registered children, found British families willing to take them, raised the required guarantees and fought the Home Office for permits. Colleagues in Prague, including Trevor Chadwick, organized the departures. Between March and August 1939 trains carried 669 children to Britain. The largest transport, set for September 1, was cancelled when war broke out, and almost none of those children survived.

Winton told almost no one. In 1988 his wife found a scrapbook in their attic with lists and photographs of the children. It led to a BBC television program in which Winton, sitting in the audience, discovered that the people around him were the children he had saved, now grown. He was knighted in 2003 and died in 2015, aged 106.
lesson: Doing good quietly, without seeking credit, can still change hundreds of lives. When you see a need nobody is meeting, start where you are with what you have.
people: Nicholas Winton, Trevor Chadwick, Grete Winton
location: Prague, Czech Republic, and London, England
source: Winton's scrapbook and records; BBC, That's Life! (February 1988); Barbara Winton, If It's Not Impossible (2014)
